title: Budget 2026 live: chancellor says scrapping of gas standing charges will save 60% of homes £45 a year

blocks.text: Getting rid of standing charges on gas bills really 'sleight of hand', Tories claim

The Conservatives have dismissed the chancellor’s decision to get rid of standing charges from energy bills just “sleight of hand”. In an interview on GB News, Richard Fuller, the shadow chief secretary to the Treasury, said:

double quotation markWe know there’s a problem with energy prices coming down the track. That’s why the Conservatives last year actually announced that cheap energy plan to get rid of VAT on people’s energy bills and roll back some of the net zero taxes that burden people’s bills. But what Labour is doing is really sleight of hand. They’re moving it from one aspect of your energy bill or your taxes, and putting it somewhere else. Under the Conservatives, of course, we would make the tougher decisions on public spending, so the actual energy bills and people’s taxes would be coming down.

blocks.caption: Richard Fuller on Sky News Photograph: Sky News

blocks.text: Green party says 'business-as-usual budget' won't deliver hope
The Green party has put out this response to the news that gas standing charges will be abolished. A spokesperson said:

double quotation markAbolishing standing charges is more tinkering from a government that is failing to take the bold action needed to end the cost of living crisis. Energy bills have skyrocketed in recent years and are set to rise by hundreds of pounds again this winter. ‘Hope’ is an easy thing to promise but will not be delivered by a business-as-usual budget.
Money saving expert Martin Lewis welcomes gas standing charge abolition, and says further energy bills support likely in budget

John Healey found time to hold a meeting with Martin Lewis, the founder of MoneySavingExpert.com, in Downing Street this morning. Lewis is one of the most trusted voices on personal finance in Britain, and he has been campaigning for standing charges to be removed from gas bills for some time.

Speaking to the media afterwards, Lewis said Healey was in a good mood. He said he asked the chancellor if there would be a support scheme to help people with energy bills from January, when costs are set to rise sharply. Lewis said Healey would not confirm anything, but he said that “reading between the lines” he gathered that there will be an announcement on this. Lewis speculated that this could be an increase in the warm homes discount, or it could be help for people in lower council tax bands.
Lewis said:

double quotation markThe biggest issue in energy right now is that we’re expecting a 27% rise in the price cap in January. I asked the Chancellor whether he will be intervening on that. He told me I’d have to wait for the budget, but reading between the lines, yes, there will be an announcement today. Whether it’s an increase in the Warm Home Discount, or whether it’s council tax band, or whether it’s done via a payout for people in say council tax bands A-D as a proxy for household income as Rishi Sunak did who knows.

blocks.text: John Healey says chancellor scrapping gas standing charges will save 60% of homes £45 a year

Good morning. When Andy Burnham became PM, he signalled that he wanted to end 40 years of neoliberalism. Judging by all the briefing about what will be in the budget today, neoliberalism is probably safe for another year or so because Burnham and his chancellor, John Healey, have decided not to use this as a moment for big, transformative change, but to instead opt for a more low-risk, every-little-bit-helps fiscal statement. There are radical elements in the Burnham agenda, but mostly they will have to wait for another day. In a video setting the scene for the budget, Healey sums it up with the slogan: “Breathing space today, and fresh hope for the future.”
Here is Pippa Crerar and Heather Stewart’s overnight splash story previewing the budget.
And here is an analysis by Phillip Inman setting out the main items we are expecting.

Every chancellor, though, likes to have at least one big surprise for the speech. This is the headline they want for tomorrow’s papers. We don’t know yet what Healey has chosen, but there is a lot of speculation that it will involve energy bills.
We have already had an announcement from the Treasury at 7am this morning about standing charges being removed from gas bills. Julia Kollewe has the story here.
According to the Treasury, this could save around 60% of families around £45 a year. It says:

The chancellor will announce today an end to this unfair and outdated practice. He will ask Ofgem to deliver removal of these charges – which are £108 a year for the typical household on average – in 2027 or as soon as possible after.
Instead, these fixed costs will be paid on the unit rate, which could save 60% of account-holding households around an average of £45 off their annual bill.

While this might sound like a modest cost of living measure – almost an “everyday fix” – Burnham and Healey – perhaps sensitive to the charge that there is not much radicalism in the budget – are presenting this as the start of something more ambitious. In a statement this morning, Burnham said this shows he’s “determined to reform our broken energy market” and Healey says:

My budget will draw a line in the sand on an energy policy that has failed British billpayers for years, letting extra costs on bills pile high and leaving households even more exposed to global shocks.

Healey is speaking at 12.30pm. We have also got PMQs today, but I will mostly be focusing on the budget, with reaction and analysis, and Graeme Wearden, who writes the Guardian’s business live blog, will be joining too to provide added firepower.
And we will also have comments open below the line (BTL).
Here is the agenda for the day.
8.45am: Andy Burnham chairs cabinet, where John Healey, the chancellor, will brief ministers on what’s in the budget.
Noon: Burnham faces Kemi Badenoch at PMQs.
12.30pm: Healey delivers the budget.
Around 1.30pm: After Healey finishes, Kemi Badenoch gives a speech responding to the budget. Other MPs respond as the budget debate continues through the afternoon.
2.30pm: Jonathan Haskel, chair of the Office for Budget Responsibility, holds a press conference.
3.30pm: Nigel Farage, the Reform UK leader, and Robert Jenrick, his Treasury spokesperson, hold a press conference to give their reaction to the budget.
